idiom_name: protocol plus protocol-extension defaults with as? capability casts (enum + exhaustive switch when the set is closed)
implementation_notes: Swift builds both halves from protocols: a protocol extension supplies the default behaviour that every visitor inherits (`extension Visitor { func visitCircle(_ c: Circle) { visitUnknown(c) } }`), an extended visitor is a protocol that inherits the first and adds a method per new element kind, and the element negotiates with a conditional cast - `if let uv = visitor as? any UnionVisitor` - falling back to the default case. Because protocols have no stored state, an implementation that wants to reuse an existing visitor's behaviour goes through a class (`class UnionArea: Area, UnionVisitor`) or holds a base visitor as a stored property; the protocol witness model documented for dynamic casting means the cast targets a protocol, and a conforming value is copied. For a closed element set the Swift answer is an enum with associated values and an exhaustive switch, which the compiler checks and which needs no accept methods at all.
pitfalls: Protocol-extension methods are statically dispatched: a method supplied only by an extension is chosen by the static type, so every visit operation that must be reachable through `any Visitor` has to be a protocol requirement, not just an extension method.

Casts into existentials succeed for any conforming type, so a visitor that conforms to the extended protocol but never intends to handle the element is indistinguishable from one that does - keep the default path explicit and throwing.

A visitor that mutates shared state during traversal must be a class or hold a reference type; `any Visitor` wraps value types by copying, so struct visitors silently lose accumulated state unless an inout or reference holder is used.
A protocol with an associated type or a Self requirement cannot be used as an existential, so the visitor protocol must be designed without them if it is to be stored and passed as `any Visitor`.
